course_title: Coding for Everyone: C and C++ Specialization

screens.title: Templates: Generic Programming
screens.subtitle: Write one blueprint that becomes many concrete types

narration.text: Generic programming is the habit of expressing algorithms and containers independent of a concrete data type. In C++, templates are the language feature that makes that possible. You will learn why templates replace duplicated functions and classes, how the compiler creates concrete code by instantiation, and what practical patterns keep templates safe and maintainable. We'll step through a familiar example — finding the maximum of two values — and show how a single template produces versions for int, double, and string. Then we'll examine class templates like a Stack to see how one definition can become distinct types such as Stack and Stack. Along the way we'll address a common stumbling block: template definitions must usually live in headers to avoid linker errors. By the end you'll understand type parameters, non-type parameters, instantiation, and a checklist for debugging cryptic template errors. Think of templates as blueprints: the same plan, reused with different materials. What piece of code in your projects could be written once as a template instead of repeated?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Templates let you write one generic definition that the compiler turns into concrete functions and classes for each used type.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will confidently explain what generic programming means and why templates are the mechanism C++ provides for it. You will implement function templates to remove duplicated logic and class templates to create reusable containers, such as a Stack or Pair, that work for any suitable type. You will also describe how the compiler performs template instantiation to produce concrete code for each used type, including how type deduction works and when you must provide explicit template arguments. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls — cryptic error messages, incorrect separation of declarations and definitions, and mistaken mixing of incompatible types — and follow best practices such as header-only templates and small, well-constrained type requirements. Each objective is tied to a practical milestone to verify competency with a short coding exercise.

screens.title: What is Generic Programming?
screens.subtitle: Algorithms and data structures written without specific types

narration.text: Generic programming is a design style in which code is written in terms of operations rather than specific types. Instead of writing separate functions for each type, you express the algorithm once and let the type vary. In C++, templates are the mechanism to express that idea. For example, before templates you might write a max function for int and another for double. Both functions do the same comparison; the only difference is the concrete type. With a function template you write one function that accepts a placeholder type parameter, and the compiler produces versions for each type you use. This reduces duplication and centralizes fixes. A helpful mental model is to think of a template as a blueprint: it contains the structure and behavior but uses parametric placeholders for the material. A common misconception is that templates are a runtime feature or a kind of polymorphism; they are not. Templates operate at compile time: the compiler generates specific code for each template use. That means templates can be as fast as handwritten code, but they also expose compile-time errors tied to how you use the type placeholders. To reinforce this, try refactoring two nearly identical functions into a single template and observe how the compiler instantiates the needed variants.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Generic programming separates algorithm from concrete type; templates are compile-time blueprints that produce specialized code for each used type.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is Generic Programming?
Core Concept

Generic programming explained

Describe algorithms in terms of operations; supply types later. Templates are compile-time blueprints, not runtime polymorphism.

Analogy
Blueprint used with different materials produces different buildings.
Misconception
Templates are not runtime virtual dispatch; they expand at compile time into concrete code.
Key Takeaway

Write once, compile many: templates remove duplication while preserving performance.

Concrete example
#include <iostream>

// Function template to find the maximum of two values
template <typename T>
T maximum(T a, T b) {
  return (a > b) ? a : b;
}

int main() {
  int i = maximum(10, 20);        // instantiates maximum<int>
  double d = maximum(3.14, 2.71); // instantiates maximum<double>
}
Why it matters
Templates enable a single verified implementation to serve many types, reducing bugs and simplifying maintenance.
Check your understanding
Can you think of two similar functions in your codebase that could be unified with a template?

screens.title: Function Templates and Instantiation
screens.subtitle: How the compiler generates concrete functions from a template

narration.text: A function template declares a family of functions parametrized by types. The template body uses a placeholder, commonly T, and the compiler instantiates concrete functions for each unique type used in calls. For a practical walkthrough, consider the maximum template. When you call the function with two integers, the compiler deduces T as int and generates an actual function maximum. When you later call maximum with doubles, maximum is generated. This instantiation happens at compile time, so there is no dynamic overhead. A common subtlety is deduction with mixed types: passing 10 and 20.5 does not deduce a single T automatically because the parameters are different types. You can fix this by explicitly specifying the template type or by converting one argument. Another point is that the template body must use only operations valid for any T your code expects; otherwise instantiation will fail for unsupported types. Misreading long template error messages is another learner hurdle; always hunt for the first error that explains an invalid operation on T. As you practice, compile small examples and force instantiations to see generated symbols and errors. This direct feedback builds intuition for when templates are a good fit and what operations your type must support.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation
keyIdea.text: The compiler deduces template parameters from calls and generates specialized functions for each used type at compile time.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Function Templates and Instantiation
Function Template

maximum<T> walkthrough

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

template <typename T>
T maximum(T a, T b) {
  return (a > b) ? a : b;
}

int main() {
  int im = maximum(10, 20);           // generates maximum<int>
  double dm = maximum(3.14, 2.71);    // generates maximum<double>
  std::string s = maximum(std::string("a"), std::string("b"));
}
Deduction caveat
Calling with mixed types prevents automatic deduction; specify the template type explicitly or cast.
Practical tip
Keep template bodies restricted to operations you know the intended types support.
Example scenario

You have two sort functions for different numeric types. Replace them with a single template and compile tests that use int and double to confirm behavior. If compilation fails for another type, check what operation is unsupported.

Common mistake
Assuming deduction will convert mixed arguments; it will not. Be explicit or cast when types differ.
Key Takeaway

Templates are instantiated per used type; deduction is convenient but has limits you must handle explicitly.

screens.title: Template Type Parameters and Deduction
screens.subtitle: How the compiler deduces T and when you must be explicit

narration.text: Template type parameters are placeholders for types that the compiler will fill in during instantiation. Deduction is the compiler's attempt to infer those types from the function arguments. The process is straightforward in uniform calls: if both parameters are int, T is int. When parameters differ, deduction can fail because a single T cannot satisfy both argument types. The mental model is a two-step process: first, the compiler parses the template definition; second, it attempts to deduce T for each use and generates specialized code. If deduction fails, you have options: convert arguments to a common type, explicitly state the template parameter, or provide overloads where necessary. This screen walks through a checklist you can follow when deduction fails: inspect argument types, try explicit template arguments, add static casts if appropriate, and consider overloads or constrained templates. A frequent beginner mistake is to attempt implicit conversions that the compiler will not perform for template deduction; be explicit. Practicing these steps will reduce surprises and help you read the first error message accurately. Template Type Parameters and Deduction means the compiler deduces type parameters from arguments, but mixed argument types may prevent deduction; explicit types or casts are needed.. In practical terms, how the compiler deduces t and when you must be explicit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deduction rules
keyIdea.text: The compiler deduces type parameters from arguments, but mixed argument types may prevent deduction; explicit types or casts are needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Template Type Parameters and Deduction
Deduction process
  1. Compiler parses the template definition without concrete types.
  2. At each call site, it tries to deduce type parameters from arguments.
  3. If a concrete type is found, it instantiates a specialized function or class for that type.
  4. If deduction fails, provide explicit template arguments or convert values.
Quick checklist when deduction fails
  • Compare actual argument types for compatibility.
  • Try an explicit template argument like maximum<double>(10, 20.5).
  • Consider overloads or casts as a last resort.
Example
maximum(10, 20.5) fails deduction. Fix: maximum<double>(10, 20.5) or cast 10 to double.
Misconception
The compiler will not silently choose a wider type for you during deduction; it needs a single consistent T.
Key Takeaway

When deduction stumbles, make the intended type explicit or align argument types so the compiler can instantiate correctly.

screens.title: Class Templates: Building Generic Containers
screens.subtitle: Define a Stack once and instantiate Stack<int>, Stack<std::string>, ...

narration.text: Class templates let you write one class blueprint that can store or manage elements of any specified type. The Stack example in the source uses a template parameter T and an internal vector of T to hold elements. When you write Stack<int>, the compiler creates a concrete class whose methods operate on int. When you write Stack<std::string>, a separate type is generated. This gives you typed containers without code duplication and enforces type safety at compile time. The class template must declare and define its member functions in a way visible to all translation units that instantiate it — which is why templates are usually header-only. A practical design tip is to limit the public interface to clear operations: push, pop, isEmpty, size. Also think about copying and exceptions; popping from an empty stack should be handled consistently. A common mistake is to attempt to instantiate a class template without providing template arguments, which the compiler rejects. Class templates scale to more sophisticated containers and are the building blocks of the standard library containers you already use, so mastering them opens up powerful reuse patterns.

keyIdea.title: Class template essence
keyIdea.text: A class template is a blueprint for a family of classes; each set of template arguments produces a distinct concrete type.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Class Templates: Building Generic Containers
Class Template Example
#include <vector>
#include <stdexcept>

template <typename T>
class Stack {
private:
  std::vector<T> elements;
public:
  void push(const T& item) { elements.push_back(item); }
  T pop() {
    if (elements.empty()) throw std::runtime_error("Stack is empty!");
    T item = elements.back(); elements.pop_back();
    return item;
  }
  bool isEmpty() const { return elements.empty(); }
  size_t size() const { return elements.size(); }
};

Instantiate as Stack<int> or Stack<std::string>. Each instantiation becomes a distinct compiled type with the same interface.

Design tips
  • Keep the interface minimal and well-documented.
  • Document type requirements: what operations T must support.
  • Handle exceptional states consistently.
Common mistake
Writing Stack without template arguments, e.g., Stack myStack; the compiler requires explicit template parameters.
Key Takeaway

Class templates provide typed containers by instantiation; design interfaces and document supported operations on the parameter types.

screens.title: Non-Type Template Parameters
screens.subtitle: Using compile-time constants as template parameters

narration.text: Templates can accept not only types but also compile-time constant values called non-type template parameters. These parameters are fixed values known at compile time, such as integers or pointers to external linkage objects. A typical example is a fixed-size array: template <typename T, size_t N> class Array { T data[N]; }; Each different N produces a distinct type, like Array<int, 10> or Array<double, 5>. This is useful when the size must be part of the type signature and known at compile time. Use non-type parameters when you need compile-time constants to influence layout or behavior without runtime overhead. A common misconception is to expect non-type parameters to accept arbitrary runtime values; they cannot. They must be constant expressions available during compilation. Also be mindful that adding non-type parameters changes type identity: Array<int,10> and Array<int,20> are different types and cannot be assigned to one another without conversion. This technique is powerful for fixed-size containers, embedded code, and compile-time optimizations. Non-Type Template Parameters means non-type template parameters are compile-time constants that become part of the type signature, enabling fixed-size or configuration-specific types.. In practical terms, using compile-time constants as template parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Non-type parameters
keyIdea.text: Non-type template parameters are compile-time constants that become part of the type signature, enabling fixed-size or configuration-specific types.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Non-Type Template Parameters
Definition

Compile-time constants as template arguments

template <typename T, size_t N>
class Array {
  T data[N];
};

// Usage:
// Array<int, 10> and Array<double, 5> are different types

Non-type parameters let the compiler place configuration into types without runtime cost. They are constrained to constant expressions and thus cannot depend on runtime input.

When to use
Fixed-size containers, compile-time tuning, or when a parameter must be part of the type identity.
Pitfall
Different non-type values create different types, preventing straightforward assignments between them.
Key Takeaway

Non-type parameters encode compile-time configuration into types for zero-cost specialization.

screens.title: Template Instantiation and Two-Phase Lookup
screens.subtitle: How definitions are parsed and checked during instantiation

narration.text: Understanding how the compiler handles templates is essential for using them correctly. The compilation model roughly follows two phases. In the first phase, the compiler parses the template definition and stores it without knowing concrete types. It checks syntax and certain context-independent constraints. In the second phase, when the template is used with specific template arguments, the compiler performs instantiation and type-checks the template body against the supplied types. At this point it validates operations on the parameter types and emits compiled code. This two-phase behavior explains why template definitions typically must be in header files: the compiler needs the body of the template available at instantiation sites so it can generate the concrete code. If definitions are hidden in a separate translation unit, other translation units attempting to instantiate the template may cause unresolved symbols during linking. A frequent learner error is to expect templates to behave like normal functions across translation units; they do not. When you read long template traces, remember they often represent many instantiations and follow-on errors; find the first instantiation that tries an invalid operation on your type. Practicing by moving definitions between header and source and observing the resulting errors builds concrete intuition about this model.

keyIdea.title: Two-phase lookup
keyIdea.text: Templates are parsed generically first; concrete type checking and code generation occur during instantiation with specific template arguments.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Template Instantiation and Two-Phase Lookup
Two-phase compilation
  1. Parsing phase: template syntax is parsed and stored without concrete types.
  2. Instantiation phase: for each use, the compiler substitutes template arguments and type-checks the body.
  3. If valid, a concrete function or class is generated and compiled.
Why header-only matters
The compiler must see the full template body at the point of instantiation. Placing definitions in headers ensures availability across translation units.
Observed symptom
Linker error like "unresolved external" often indicates template definitions are hidden in a .cpp while instantiations occur elsewhere.
Debug tip
Find the first error in a long trace — it usually pinpoints the invalid use of the template parameter.
Key Takeaway

Templates are compiled in two phases; ensure definitions are visible at instantiation time to avoid linker and instantiation errors.

screens.title: Header-Only Templates vs Separate Definitions
screens.subtitle: Why template implementations usually live in headers

narration.text: A frequent source of confusion is whether template declarations and definitions can be separated like ordinary classes and functions. For templates, separation commonly causes linker errors. When you declare a template in a header but put its definition in a. cpp, other translation units that include the header do not see the implementation when they instantiate the template. The compiler needs the full definition to perform instantiation at compile time. If it cannot instantiate, the expected symbols are missing at link time, producing unresolved external errors. The practical rule is to place both declaration and definition together, typically in a header file, or to use an included implementation file pattern where the. ipp or. tpp file is included at the end of the header. The comparison here is simple: header-only templates expose the body at instantiation sites and avoid linker surprises; separated definitions hide the implementation and require explicit instantiation in every translation unit that needs a concrete type. Be careful: explicit instantiation is possible but cumbersome, so prefer header-only for general template code. When you see linker errors, check whether template definitions are visible where instantiation happens.

keyIdea.title: Header-only rule
keyIdea.text: Templates usually must have definitions visible at instantiation; keep implementations in headers or include implementation files from headers to avoid linker errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Header-Only Templates vs Separate Definitions
Header-only
  • Definitions are in headers, visible at instantiation.
  • Compiler can generate concrete types where needed.
  • Preferred default for general templates.
Separate .cpp
  • Hiding definitions in .cpp causes link-time unresolved symbols for instantiations in other translation units.
  • Explicit instantiation is an advanced alternative but often impractical.
Practice note
If you must separate, either provide explicit instantiations for all needed combinations in the implementation file or include the implementation into the header so the compiler can instantiate as needed.
Key Takeaway

Prefer header-only templates so the compiler can instantiate templates where they are used; separate definitions commonly cause linker errors.

screens.title: Reading Template Error Messages
screens.subtitle: Find the first error and inspect the invalid operation on T

narration.text: Template diagnostics can be long and intimidating, but there is a reliable approach to make them useful. First, locate the earliest error in the trace — later lines are frequently consequences of the first failure. That first error usually points at an operation inside the template body that is invalid for the instantiated type. For example, if you call a member function on T that only exists for some types, instantiation for other types will fail at that call. When you encounter such an error, inspect the operation and document the requirements on T: which expressions must be valid, which operators must be supported, and whether the type must be copyable or movable. Another useful technique is to force instantiation with a known type and compile repeatedly while narrowing the failing expression. Avoid overreacting to template noise: focus on the concrete operation at the first failure. Also consider adding static_assert checks with readable messages to enforce requirements early. Over time you'll learn to map error patterns to common problems: missing operations, incorrect overloads, or visibility issues due to two-phase lookup. These strategies make template debugging systematic rather than mysterious.

keyIdea.title: Debug strategy
keyIdea.text: Identify the first error in the diagnostics and analyze which operation on the template parameter is invalid for the instantiated type.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Reading Template Error Messages
Diagnostic workflow
  1. Find the earliest error line in the compiler output.
  2. Read the operation that failed inside the template body.
  3. Determine the requirements on the template parameter type.
  4. Adjust code, add casts, or constrain the template accordingly.
Tip
Insert static_assert with type traits or clear messages to detect missing capabilities earlier and improve diagnostics readability.
Common patterns
  • Missing operator> or missing member function.
  • Invalid conversion between template and argument types.
Practice
Force an instantiation with a failing type and read the first reported error to identify the broken expression.
Key Takeaway

Treat long template traces like trees: the first root error explains the rest. Use assertions and small reproductions to isolate the problem.

narration.text: The Pair class exercise is a focused way to practice class templates. The goal is to create a template that stores two potentially different types, T1 and T2, and provides getters and setters. Start by declaring template <typename T1, typename T2> class Pair with private members first and second. Implement a constructor that initializes both members by value or const reference. Provide getFirst and getSecond methods marked const to return copies or const references depending on your design. Add setFirst and setSecond to modify values. Test by instantiating Pair<int, double>, Pair<std::string, bool>, and Pair<int, int> and calling getters and setters to verify behavior. A common beginner pitfall is returning references to temporaries or exposing internal state unintentionally; prefer copying or const references and document your choice. Keep the implementation in a header or include the implementation file to avoid linker errors. This straightforward exercise checks your ability to declare template parameters, define member functions, and instantiate class templates across types. Implementing a Generic Pair Class means implement a two-parameter class template with constructor, getters, setters, and tests for multiple type combinations.. In practical terms, step-by-step guidance and starter code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pair exercise
keyIdea.text: Implement a two-parameter class template with constructor, getters, setters, and tests for multiple type combinations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Implementing a Generic Pair Class
Starter code
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

// Define the class template Pair
template <typename T1, typename T2>
class Pair {
private:
  T1 first;
  T2 second;
public:
  Pair(T1 f, T2 s) : first(f), second(s) {}
  T1 getFirst() const { return first; }
  T2 getSecond() const { return second; }
  void setFirst(T1 f) { first = f; }
  void setSecond(T2 s) { second = s; }
};

int main() {
  Pair<int, double> p1(10, 20.5);
  std::cout << p1.getFirst() << ", " << p1.getSecond() << std::endl;
}
Test multiple type combinations and ensure getters and setters behave as expected. Keep the template in a header to allow instantiation across translation units.
Common pitfalls
  • Returning references to local temporaries.
  • Forgetting template parameters when instantiating the class.
Extension
Add move semantics or const-reference getters for efficiency and document behavior for large types.
Key Takeaway

Implementing Pair reinforces class templates, constructor initialization, and safe getter/setter design across types.

screens.title: Best Practices and When to Use Templates
screens.subtitle: Guidelines for maintainable and safe generic code

narration.text: Templates are powerful, but they come with design responsibilities. Use templates when you need compile-time type flexibility without runtime overhead — for containers, algorithms, and utilities that apply to multiple types. Keep templates small and focused, document the required operations on type parameters, and prefer header-only implementations unless you have a disciplined explicit-instantiation strategy. Favor simple type requirements: prefer that T is copyable, comparable, or supports the operations you need. Use static_assert and type traits to provide clearer diagnostic messages when requirements are not met. Avoid embedding complex logic that depends on subtle type-specific behavior; consider overloads or concept-based constraints when available. When debugging, isolate failing instantiations into small test programs to get clearer errors. Remember that the Standard Template Library is built on templates; use it as a model for interface design and naming. Finally, balance reuse against clarity: templates can obscure intent if overused. Ask whether a template variant truly reduces duplication and improves clarity for other developers before generalizing a function or class. Best Practices and When to Use Templates means prefer small, well-documented templates, header-only definitions, clear type requirements, and targeted use where compile-time flexibility adds value.. In practical terms, guidelines for maintainable and safe generic code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice rules
keyIdea.text: Prefer small, well-documented templates, header-only definitions, clear type requirements, and targeted use where compile-time flexibility adds value.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Best Practices and When to Use Templates
Guidelines
  • Use templates for compile-time flexibility and zero-cost abstractions.
  • Document required operations on type parameters clearly.
  • Prefer header-only implementation to avoid linker issues.
  • Add static_asserts and type-trait checks to improve diagnostics.
When not to template
If the generic version complicates the API or hides intent, prefer a well-named family of concrete functions instead of over-generalizing.
Design check
Ask: Does generalizing reduce duplication and improve clarity? If yes, template may be appropriate.
Reference
Study STL container interfaces for examples of clear, reusable template design.
Key Takeaway

Use templates deliberately: they deliver reuse and performance but require clear contracts and header visibility for reliable compilation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Templates: Generic Programming

narration.text: Here are the compact ideas to carry forward. First, generic programming means writing algorithms and containers independent of concrete types; templates are the C++ mechanism for that. Second, function templates let one definition serve many types via compiler instantiation, while class templates let you define containers like Stack that become distinct typed classes when instantiated. Third, templates accept not only types but also non-type compile-time parameters that make configuration part of the type identity. Fourth, instantiation and two-phase lookup mean the compiler needs the template body at use sites, which is why templates are usually header-only. Fifth, template error messages are often verbose; find the first error and inspect the invalid operation on the template parameter. Finally, adopt best practices: keep templates focused, document type requirements, and use static_asserts or traits to improve diagnostics. These points form the foundation for working effectively with C++ templates.

keyIdea.title: Three quick cards
keyIdea.text: Templates = blueprints. Instantiation = compile-time generation. Header-only = practical necessity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Generic Programming
Write algorithms independent of concrete types to reduce duplication.
Templates
Templates are blueprints the compiler uses to generate concrete functions and classes.
Header-Only
Keep template definitions visible at instantiation to avoid linker errors.
Summary takeaway
Templates give you reusable, type-safe code when used with clear contracts and header visibility. Practice with small examples to build confidence reading instantiation traces.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to guide your work with templates

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders in mind. First, templates are compile-time blueprints — they create specialized code for each type you use and are not runtime polymorphism. Second, always ensure template definitions are visible where they are instantiated; prefer header-only or include implementation files from headers to avoid linker problems. Third, when you read template error messages, find the first reported failure and map it to the invalid operation on the template parameter. These habits will reduce common mistakes and help you adopt templates safely in real projects. Practice by refactoring a duplicated function into a template, implementing the Pair or Stack exercises, and intentionally causing a deduction or linker error to build debugging skill. That direct practice cements both the concept and the practical techniques for maintaining robust generic code.

keyIdea.text: Templates = compile-time blueprints; header-only definitions; diagnose by locating the first error.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What to Remember
Compile-time blueprints
Templates generate concrete code per type at compile time.
Header visibility
Keep definitions visible where instantiation occurs to avoid linker errors.
Diagnose by the first error
The earliest reported error usually reveals the invalid operation on the template parameter.
Final thought
Practice small refactors into templates and deliberate errors to build skill reading traces and writing clear, reusable generic code.

ai_generation_note:
Create an 11-14 minute video lesson with a strong visual emphasis on template instantiation. Start with the problem of code duplication (e.g., `max_int`, `max_double`) and then introduce function templates as the solution. Use animated code snippets to show `template <typename T>` and how `T` is replaced by `int`, `double`, `std::string` during instantiation. Transition to class templates with the `Stack` example, visualizing how `Stack<int>` and `Stack<std::string>` are distinct types generated from the same blueprint. Include a dedicated segment on the "header-only" rule for templates, using diagrams to explain why separating declaration and definition into `.h` and `.cpp` files leads to linker errors, and how putting everything in `.h` resolves it. The interactive element could be a mini-quiz where learners identify correct and incorrect template usage scenarios (e.g., missing template arguments for a class template).
